M Amir-ul Islam with Tania Amir and Manjill Murshed, Advocates ------ For the Petitioner. 
Abdur Razaque, Additional Attorney-General with Abdul Awal, Deputy Attorney-General, ABM Waliur Rahman Khan and Fahima Nasren, Assistant Attorney-General ---- For the State.
parties:
Zilaluddin (Md) ----- Petitioner
Vs.
Secretary, Ministry of Home Affairs and others ----- Respondents
full_judgment:
3. Mr M Amirul Islam, the learned Counsel for the petitioner, submits that the allegation as made in the ground of detention are vague, indefinite and unspecified which cannot at all be considered to be sufficient grounds for detention of the detenu and, as such, he should be released from detention. He submits that the detenu has been implicated in the case out of political rivalry though he is in no way connected with the case. He further submits that the detenu was not placed /produced before the Advisory Board within 120 days from the date of the order of detention as required under section 10 of the Special Powers Act, 1974 and noncompliance of this mandatory provision of law renders the detention order illegal for which the detenu should be released from detention. 

 4. Mr A Awal, the learned Deputy Attorney-General, opposes the Rule by filing a supplementary affidavit and counter-affidavit stating, inter alia, that there is specific allegation against the detenu to the effect that on 17-6-2001 while the Chairperson of the Bangladesh Nationalist Party and leader of the Opposition Begum Khaleda Zia was proceeding towards Pirojpur by road with motorcade and reached near the place known as Kadampur, the detenu along with his accomplices being armed with lethal weapons including firearms pounced on the motorcade and the tires of two buses of her security were punctured in the attack made by firearms and also fired indiscriminately upon the said motorcade and created a barricade on the road and thus such environment created a panic endangering the life of the Chairperson including others who accompanied her and in considering the nature of the offence, which was in fact serious, this Court in an earlier case being Criminal Miscellaneous Case No. 521 of 2002 filed by the same petitioner, discharged the Rule holding that the grounds were not vague, indefinite and unspecified and that the detaining authority was justified in detaining the detenu in considering the nature of the offence which was serious. He submits that the case records of the detenu was received by the Secretary, Advisory Board in the Ministry of Home Affairs on 27-4-02 and the order recommending further detention of the detenu by the Advisory Board was passed on 15-5-2002 when the case record with detenu was placed/produced before the Board. He submits that the date of receipt of the case records by the Secretary, Advisory Board tantamounts placing of the same before the Advisory Board and that since the case records was received on the 116th day (Jan-30+Feb-28+Mar. 31+April. 27=116) from the date of the order of detention, so it cannot be said that the case records of the detenu or the detenu as the case may be, was not placed/produced before the Advisory Board within 120 days as required under section 10 of the Special Powers Act, 1974 and, as such, the Rule should be discharged. 

 5. The crux of the point is, whether the detenu or the case records of the detenu was, in fact, placed/produced before the Advisory Board within 120 days from the date of order of detention dated 2-1-2002 as required under section 10 of the Special Powers Act, 1974. Section 10 of the Special Power Act, 1974 runs as follows: 

 "In every case where a detention order has been made under this Act, the government shall within one hundred and twenty days from the date of detention under the order, place before the Advisory Board constituted under section 9 the grounds on which the order has been made and the representation if any made by the person affected by the order." 

 6. This section provides for placing the case records of the detenu before the Advisory Board within 120 days from the date of the order of detention. There is no ambiguity in this section regarding placing the case records of the detenu before the Advisory Board within 120 days from the date of order of detention. In this case the case records of the detenu along with the detenu was placed before the Advisory Board on 15-5-2002 (Annexure-1) of the Supplementary Affidavit filed on behalf of the opposite party State. So, it is clear that the case records of the detenu along with the detenu was not placed before the Advisory Board within 120 days. The case records and the detenu was placed before the Advisory Board on 15-5-2002 (Jan. 30 +Feb. 28+March 31+Apr.30+May. 15=134) on 134th day from the date of order of detention and not within 120 days as required under section 10 of the Special Powers Act, 1974. Receipt of the case records of the detenu (Annexure-1) of the supplementary Affidavit by the Secretary of the Advisory Board in the Ministry of Home Affairs cannot in any way be construed placing of the same before the Advisory Board as contemplated under section 10 of the Special Powers Act. It appears from the Movement Register produced with the confidential file of the detenu that the case records of the detenu bearing Number 2/2002 from the office of the Deputy Commissioner, Dhaka was received by the concerned official of the Advisory Board in the Ministry of Home Affairs on 27-4-2002. 'But the case records of the detenu as I have already stated was not placed/produced before the Advisory Board prior to 15-5-2002 as there is nothing to show that the case records of the detenu was either placed/produced before the Advisory Board on 27-4-2002 or on any other date within 1st of May, 2002 and, as such, the order dated 30-5-2002 issued by the Government extending the detention order for 3 more months with effect from 29-6-2002 with the Approval of the Advisory Board cannot but be said to be illegal for which the Rule should be made absolute and the detenu should be released from detention as it is the consistent decisions of this court that if the case records of the detenu or the detenu as the case may be is not placed/produced before the Advisory Board within 120 days from the date of the order of detention as required under section 10 of the Special Powers Act, 1974. then the detention order becomes illegal. The contention of the learned Deputy Attorney-General that the date of receipt of the case records of the detenu by the official of the Advisory Board in the Ministry of Home Affairs is also the date of placing of the case records of the detenu before the Advisory Board is a fallacious one and does not stand to reason and, as such, I have no hesitation to hold that the case records of the detenu was not placed/produced before the Advisory Board within 1st May, 2002 i.e. within 120th day from the date of the order of detention as constituted under section 9 of the Special Powers Act, 1974. 

 8. Be that as it may, the order dated 30-5-2002 issued by the Government extending the order of detention of the detenu for 3 months with effect from 29-6-2002 on the basis of the recommendation made by the Advisory Board on 15-5-2002 is declared illegal as the case records of the detenu or the detenu as the case may be was not placed /produced before the Advisory Board within 120 days from the date of the order of detention as provided under section 10 of the Special Powers Act, 1974 and, as such, the detenu is entitled to 'be released from detention though earlier in Criminal Miscellaneous Case No. 521 of 2002 (in which I was the author Judge) the detention order of the detenu was found legal and proper and the Rule was discharged in considering the facts and circumstance of the case. 

 9. In the result, the Rule is made absolute. Let the detenu Mahbubur Rahman son of late Abdul Malek of Abdullahpur West Para, Keranigonj, Dhaka now detained in Dhaka Central Jail, Dhaka be set at liberty at once, if not wanted in connection with any other case. 

 Md Shamsul Huda J: I have the opportunity to hear my learned brother pronouncing judgment in this Criminal Miscellaneous Case. I regret that I could not agree to the decisions finally arrived at by my learned brother making the Rule absolute and releasing the detenu from detention and, as such, I, propose to deliver a separate judgment. 

 11. For avoiding repetition of facts I shall just mention below the facts of the case briefly. Detenu Mahbubur Rahman was arrested under section 54 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and subsequently he was shown arrested in Keranigonj PS Case No. 17 dated 14-1-02 instituted upon FIR being lodged on 17-6-2001 by one Haji Nazamuddin on an allegation that on 17-6-2001 while Chairperson of Bangladesh Nationalist Party and the then leader of the Opposition Begum Khaleda Zia was proceeding towards Pirojpur by road and reached near Kadampur, on the way from Dhaka to Mowa ferry ghat, the detenu along with his other accomplices being armed with weapons and firearms attacked the motorcade and opened fire indiscriminately upon the same, endangering lives of Begum Khaleda Zia and her companions and caused damage to some buses and obstructed in her lawful political activities and also there is an allegation against him that he is a terrorist, extortionist, and due to his illegal activities the normal life of the people of the locality became jeopardised. On the above grounds, the District Magistrate, Dhaka issued detention order dated 2-1-2002 under section 3(2) of the Special Powers Act 1974, detaining him for 30 days and the grounds of detention was duly served upon him. The detention order was subsequently extended by the Government for further period of 3(three) months with effect from 2-2-2002 which was challenged by an application under section 491 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, vide Criminal Miscellaneous Case No. 521 of 2002 (arising out of Miscellaneous Case No. 11 of 2002) and upon hearing the parties by a Division Bench of this court being presided over by my learned Brother Mr Justice Md Ali Asgar Khan, discharged the Rule by judgment dated 5-3-2002 finding that the order of detention was legal and the allegations made in the grounds of detention are serious in nature which comes under the purview of the definition of prejudicial act. Thereafter, the Government extended the order of detention for a period of 3(three) months with effect from 1-5-2002 And copy of such order was duly served upon the detenu. The instant Criminal Miscellaneous Case No. 5045 of 2002 under section 491 of the Code of Criminal Procedure was filed challenging the aforesaid order of extension of .detention order, passed by the Government, vide Annexure-1 to the petition, upon which Rule was issued. In the petition under section 491 of the Code of Criminal Procedure the petitioner challenged the order of detention of detenu Mahbubur Rahman, mainly on the ground that the detenu has not been placed before the Advisory Board within 120 days from the date of initial order of detention as per provision of section 10 of the Special Powers Act, 1974. 

 "In every case where a detention order has been made under this Act, the Government shall, within one hundred and twenty days from the date of detention under the order, place before the Advisory Board constituted under section 9 the grounds on which the order has been made and the representation, if any, made by the person affected by the order." 

 21. The submission of Mr Islam, learned Senior Counsel for the petitioner that the Secretary of the Advisory Board being an employee and official of the Ministry of Home Affairs is not an authorised person to receive the grounds on behalf of the Advisory Board is not sustainable. I do not find any such restriction, because the Governments got "Rules of Business" where allocation of powers and duties of each and every government official has been specified. The position of the Secretary of the Advisory Board has been misconstrued and misconceived as the Secretary of Ministry of Home Affairs. The learned Deputy Attorney-General produced before us the official Register of the Advisory Board wherein it is found that in each and every case the Secretary of the Board used to receive the grounds and then the Board proceeds in accordance with law. Section 12(2) of the Special Powers Act provides as follows: 

 In any case where the Advisory Board has reported that there is, in its opinion, sufficient cause for the detention of a person the Government may confirm the detention order and continue the detention of the person concerned for such period as it thinks fit." 

 22. After receiving the grounds of detention by the Secretary of the Advisory Board, fixing date of hearing and observing other necessary legal formalities are the internal proceeding of the Advisory Board and this court should not sit as a court of Appeal on the internal proceeding of the Advisory Board, except considering the fact that whether the Advisory Board forwarded its opinion to the Government within 170 days. Section 10 of the Act provides that Government shall place the grounds of detention before the Advisory Board within 120 days. In this case the Government has done so but as to when the materials were considered, it is beyond the scope of our scrutiny, as the internal proceeding of the Advisory Board is not before us. 

 24. Mr Islam has further strenuously argued that this is a new invention of the Advisory Board, being presided over by a Senior Judge of the High Court Division that they have passed the order of detention. The detenu has been languishing in jail under the said order which is illegal and ultra vires as being passed by the learned Judges of the High Court Division It is shocking that facts are not properly placed before the court. In his argument Mr Islam submitted that the Government neither confirmed nor issued fresh order of detention. On the other hand, Mr A Awal, the learned Deputy Attorney-General, has placed before us the order of detention dated 30-5-2002 being issued by the Senior Assistant Secretary (নিরাপত্তা শাখা-৩) Ministry of Home Affairs pursuant to the opinion of the Advisory Board and the said detention order was received by the detenu on 3-6-2002, copy of which has also been kept in the confidential file. With due respect I must mention here that this type of submission sometimes misleads the court in taking proper decision. I feel obliged to mention that it is the duty of the petitioner to place the fact properly before the Court, then the opposite party has responsibility to controvert the same if required. It is the established principle of law but I regret to observe that in this case there is serious lapse in placing the facts before the court. 

 (Criminal Miscellaneous Jurisdiction) 

 Criminal Miscellaneous Case No. 5045 of 2002 

 In this criminal miscellaneous case under section 491 of the Code of Criminal Procedure the detention of detenu Mahbubor Rahman son of late Abdul Malek of Abdullahpur Westpara, Keraniganj, District Dhaka has been challenged. The Miscellaneous case was heard by a Division Bench comprising of their Lordships' Mr Justice Md Ali Asgar Khan and Mr Justice Shamsul Huda and their Lordships gave dissenting judgments. Mr Justice Md Ali Asgar Khan made the Rule absolute declaring the order dated 30-5-2002 issued by the Government extending the order of detention of the detenu for 3(three) months with effect from 29-6-2002 on the basis of the recommendation made by the Advisory Board on 15-5-2002 illegal as the case records of the detenu or the detenu as the case may be was not placed/produced before the Advisory Board within 120 days from the date of the order of detention as provided in section 10 of the Special Powers Act, 1974 (hereinafter referred to as the Act) and accordingly, ordered to set the detenu at liberty at once, if not wanted in connection with any other case. Although Mr Md Ali Asgar Khan J has not given any decision as to the maintainability of the miscellaneous case, yet, it has to be presumed that his Lordship found the miscellaneous case maintainable, otherwise, his Lordship would not have made the Rule absolute on merit. 

 2. Mr Md Shamsul Huda J, discharged the Rule holding, the view that the order of extension-dated 30-5-2002 has been issued by the government in accordance with the provision of law and no illegality has been committed by the Advisory Board in passing its opinion. The grounds of detention having been received by the Secretary of the Advisory Board within 120 days from the date of the order of detention the same to be treated for placement 'before the Advisory Board itself within the prescribed time within the meaning of section 10 of the Act. His Lordship has also held that there is no provision or rule in sections 10 and 11 of the Act that the detenu must be produced before the Advisory Board within 120 days from the date of the order of detention except the grounds of detention. Mr Md Shamsul Huda J, also found the miscellaneous case not maintainable holding as under; 

 3. As the two learned Judges dissented in delivering the judgments in the manner as aforementioned, the learned Chief Justice has sent the miscellaneous case to me for hearing and disposal as a Third Judge and accordingly the Rule has been heard by me on 24-7-2002 and judgment is being delivered today. 

 4. As there is no dispute as to the material facts involved in the case and my learned Brothers in their dissenting judgments have already stated the facts in detail, I do not like to restate the facts just to make the judgment a lengthy one, except the dates of making the order of detention upon the detenu, service of the order of detention, the extension of the order of detention from time to time and the placement of the grounds of detention before the Advisory Board as contended by the Government. The order of detention dated 2-1-2002 was issued by the Additional District Magistrate, Dhaka under section 3(2) of the Act for the preventive detention of the detenu for a period of 30(thirty) days. The grounds of detention were served upon the detenu on 15-1-2002. The order or detention was extended by the government under section 3(3) of the Act, for a further period of 3 months with effect from 2-2-2002. Subsequently, the government in exercise of its power under section 3(1)(a) of the Act, issued an order of detention on 22-4-2002 for a further period of 60 days with effect from 1-5-2002 and lastly, extended the order of detention for a further period of 3(three) months with effect from 29-6-2002 on the basis of recommendation made by the Advisory Board dated 15-5-2002. It is also necessary to state that earlier Criminal Miscellaneous Case No. 521 of 2002 was filed before this court challenging the initial order of detention and a Division Bench presided over by Mr Md Ali Asgar Khan, J, discharged the Rule by judgment and order dated 5-3-2002, holding that the order of detention passed against the detenu was legal and proper. 

 5. In this miscellaneous case the order of detention dated 22-4-2002 vide Memo No. 1343 Sha:Ma. (Nira-3) issued by respondent No. 3, namely, the Assistant Secretary, Secret Section 3, Ministry of Home Affairs has been challenged. In the application various contentions have been raised but all those are not necessary to be restated for the disposal of the contentious points now before me, because of the dissenting judgments passed by the two learned Judges as indicated hereinabove, and in view of the decisions passed in the said Criminal Miscellaneous Case No. 521 of 2002. 

 8. Mr M Amirul Islam, the learned Advocate appearing in support of the application, submits that neither the grounds of detention nor the detenue having been placed before the Advisory Board within 120 days from the date of the order of detention as mandated by section 10 of the Act, the order of detention has become illegal and the detenue is being detained in custody illegally and, as such, he is entitled to be set at liberty. Mr M Amirul Islam submits that 'Advisory Board' contemplated in section 9 of the Act has been borrowed from clause (4) of Article 33 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh, which speaks of an Advisory Board consisting of three persons, of whom two shall be persons who are, or have been, or are qualified to be appointed as, judges of the Supreme Court and the other shall be a person who is a Senior Officer in the Service of the Republic, the contention of the State that the grounds of detention having been referred to by the government to the Advisory Board which was received by its Secretary on 27-4-2002, that is on 116th day from the date of the order of detention, there was compliance of the mandatory provision of section 10 of the Act cannot be accepted. Mr M Amirul Islam further submits that sections 9, 10 and 11 of the Act have to be read together in order to give a harmonious meaning and if these sections are read together it will appear that the concept of "Secretary of the Advisory Board' as contended by the State is foreign to these sections and, as such, it cannot be said that the so-called receipt of the grounds of detention by the Secretary of the Advisory Board is a compliance of the mandatory provision of section 10 of the Act. He further submits that section 11 of the Act has laid down the procedure to be followed by the Advisory Board and in this section there are two clauses, first one provides for consideration of the materials placed before it by the government and calling for such further information as it may deem necessary from the government and the second one, or hearing the detenu in person and then to submit its report to the government within one hundred and seventy days from the date of detention. And he continues to submit that the said two clauses separated by the word 'or' have to be read conjunctively which means that both, the grounds of detention and the detenue have to be placed before the Advisory Board within one hundred and twenty days, otherwise, if the word 'or' is read disjunctively then only the grounds of detention shall have to be placed before the Advisory Board and in that case the detenue will be deprived of hearing and thereby the government will be given a handle to place the materials and information of its own choice before the Advisory Board, which will make the purpose of placement and consideration of the materials as contemplated in sections 10 and 11 of the Act ineffective and meaningless. Mr M Amirul Islam lastly, submits by referring to Annexure-II to the supplementary affidavit that it is a printed form in which the opinion of the Advisory Board has been written and that too only in respect of the satisfaction as to the presence of grounds of detention for keeping the detenu under detention without having any reflection as to the absence of the grounds for not keeping the detenu in detention, and, as such, the same does not comply with the provision of section 11 of the Act, which makes the opinion of the Advisory Board mechanical and shows non-application of its mind and, as such, the detenu cannot be detained in custody on the basis of the recommendation of the Advisory Board. 

 10: Let me first consider the question as to whether the criminal miscellaneous case is maintainable in' law for want of statements in the application as to the locus standi of the petitioner to challenge the order of detention passed against the detenu and as to how he is aggrieved by .the order of  detention passed against the detenu: If the miscellaneous case is not found maintainable in law as held by my brother Mr Shamsul Huda J, then there would be no need to discuss and decide the points raised by the learned Advocates noted there in before, as in that case it would be mere academic to decide the said points which has been discouraged by the Appellate Division in number of cases. Section 491 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (hereinafter referred to as the Code) is in Part VIII under the head Special Proceedings and chapter has been attributed to it under the head ''Directions of the Nature of Habeas Corpus' (all the underlinings hereinafter have been made by me to put emphasis). 

 The jurisdiction of the court vested under this section is absolutely distinct and different from that of the writ of habeas corpus as contemplated in Article 102 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh which was framed in 1972. Section 491 of the Code is a pre-constitutional piece of legislation. The striking distinct feature is that Clause 2(b) of Article 102 of the Constitution which provides for the writ of the nature of habeas corpus starts with the words 'on the application of any person make an order'. Whereas, sub-section 1 of section 491 of the Code opens with the words "The High Court Division may, whenever it thinks fit, direct……” The expression 'whenever it thinks fit' confers an absolute discretion on the court to exercise its power thereunder or not to do so, having regard to the circumstances of each case. There is also no specific form for a petition under this section. But, as .a general rule, however, any person having special interest, right, or authority in or from the person wrongfully detained may seek relief on his behalf. Therefore, an application can be made by his wife, or a friend or some other relation and a statement should be made in the application in that respect. The reason being that the application must contain the full particulars of the detenu and the detention. Here, in this case, although, in the application no statement has been made as to the relationship of the petitioner with the detenu and as to how he is aggrieved, yet, full particulars of the detenu and detention have been given and the court has got no difficulty to know the facts and the circumstances of the case to exercise its discretion. I am of the view that an application made under this section cannot be rejected simply on the ground that no statement has been made in the application as to the locus standi of the petitioner to challenge the order of detention or as to how the petitioner is aggrieved by the order of detention, if full particulars of the detenu and the detention are there. By now it is a well settled proposition of law that even the High Court Division can suo motu interfere, when it comes to its knowledge that liberty of a citizen had been taken away by the detaining authority without lawful authority and a citizen is being detained in public or private custody within its limit illegally or improperly. I am also of the further view that the court cannot decline to act at once to restore the liberty of a citizen so taken, on the ground of technicality. More so, when the High Court Division entertained the application and issued Rule and the State did not raise any objection either in the counter-affidavit or in the supplementary affidavit as to the maintainability of the application filed by-the petitioner on behalf of the detenue. In conclusion, I hold that the miscellaneous case is maintainable in law. 

 11. In view of the submissions made by the learned Additional Attorney-General to the effect that the Secretary of the Advisory Board having received the grounds of detention on 27-4-2002, that is on 116th day from the date of the order of detention section10 of the Act was complied with, I wanted to know from him as to how the Secretary of the Advisory Board was appointed or who appointed whom. The learned Additional Attorney-General could - not give any satisfactory reply and sought for some time and accordingly, the miscellaneous case was kept for judgment today, just to allow him time to apprise me in that respect. A supplementary affidavit has been filed by the State today, affidavit of which has been sworn in by Hamida Chowdhury, styling herself as Secretary of the Advisory Board stating, inter alia, that she joined as a Member of Bangladesh Civil Service (Administration) Cadre in 1993 and eventually has been posted as the Senior Assistant Secretary, Ministry of Home Affairs in the year 2000 dealing with the detention cases and she was given an additional charge to perform as the Secretary of the Advisory Board vide letter being Memo No. 20 Sha-Ma-(Prasha-1) Neog-24194-397 dated 14-5-2001, and since then she has been performing the said job of maintaining liaison with the Advisory Board. It has also been stated that in discharging her duty she has been acting as coordinator for and on behalf of the Advisory Board. The relevant files are regularly brought to the notice of the Chairman and the Members of the Advisory Board and subject to their convenience the Advisory Board sits in the Supreme Court Building Ejlash of the Chairman and each detenu is afforded with the opportunity of being heard. She has further asserted, that according to the records available with her she ascertained that the aforesaid practice and procedure are being followed since 1974 and the office orders in that respect from 1980 have been annexed as Annexures-III and IV series. 

 18. So far as the Act is concerned it is silent as .to how the Advisory Board shall work or function. But, in view of the discussions made above, I am of the view that it is the Advisory Board which will decide as to how it shall function or work in order to discharge its statutory obligations as conferred by section 11 of the Act, but whatever may be the modus operandi that must not be in violation of the provisions of sections 10 and 11 of the Act as discussed and observed hereinabove. I am also of the view that the questions involved in this miscellaneous case being as to the functioning or working of a composite body constituted under section 9 of the Act, namely, 'Advisory Board' in order to carry out the mandates of law as required. by sections 10 and 11 of the Act, the Rules of Business has nothing to do. 

 In the result, the Rule is made absolute. Let the detenu Mahbubur Rahman son of the late Abdul Malek of Abdullahpur, West Para, Keraniganj, Dhaka now detained in Dhaka Central Jail, Dhaka be set as liberty at once, if not wanted in connection with any other case.
